data.title: Unrestricted File Upload Leading to Remote Code Execution
data.summary:
An upload function accepted files of arbitrary type and stored them in a location
from which the web server executed them, allowing arbitrary commands to be run on
the underlying host.
data.description:
The application provided a file upload function intended for documents and
images. No validation was performed on the file extension, the declared content
type, or the file signature, and uploaded files were written to a directory
within the web root that remained directly reachable over HTTP.

As a result, a file carrying an extension handled by the server-side interpreter
was executed rather than served as static content. This lets the uploader run arbitrary commands in the security context of the account under
which the web service runs.

Where validation is implemented solely on the client, it provides no protection,
as an attacker submits the request directly and never executes the client-side
code. Validation based on the declared content type is likewise ineffective,
since that value is supplied by the requester.

The issue was confirmed by uploading a file containing server-side code and
observing its execution.
data.impact:
An attacker could execute arbitrary commands on the web server, obtaining access
to the application's source code, configuration files, and any credentials they
contain, as well as the data held by connected systems. This establishes a
foothold within the internal network from which further systems can be attacked,
and represents complete compromise of the affected host.
data.recommendation:
1. Validate uploaded files against an allowlist of permitted extensions on the
   server side. Deny by default and permit only the specific types the business
   function requires; denylists are consistently bypassed.

2. Verify the file signature rather than relying on the extension or the declared
   content type, both of which are controlled by the requester.

3. Store uploaded files outside the web root and serve them through a handler
   that sets an appropriate content type and content disposition, so that the
   server never interprets uploaded content as executable.

4. Rename uploaded files to randomly generated values on receipt, discarding the
   original name, to prevent extension manipulation and path traversal.

5. Disable script execution in any directory that receives uploaded content
   through web server configuration, as a defence-in-depth control.

6. Run the web service under a dedicated low-privileged account with no rights
   beyond those it requires, limiting the impact should the controls above fail.
